title_en: Beijing New Aote Company v. Huarong Company — dispute over equity transfer contract
ruling_gist_en: Due to the fault of both parties, which led to the termination of performance of the equity transfer agreement, the losses incurred by one party in preparation for and actual performance of the agreement shall be jointly borne by both parties as civil liability.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over equity transfer contract; Second instance; Supreme People's Court; Beijing City; Legal person; Contract Law; Liability for termination of performance of equity transfer agreement; Bearing of losses; Partial support; Equity transfer; Right of first refusal; Arbitral award; Good faith; Contract dispute; Dispute over equity transfer contract of Huarong Company
full_text_en:
Beijing Xin'ao'te Group Co., Ltd. v. China Huarong Asset Management Corporation — dispute over equity transfer contract

Ruling Summary

Where both parties are at fault, causing the termination of performance of an equity transfer agreement, the losses incurred by one party in preparing for and actually performing the agreement shall be borne jointly by both parties.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court
(2003) Min Er Zhong Zi No. 143

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Beijing Xin'ao'te Group Co., Ltd. Domicile: 6th Floor, Silicon Valley Computer City, No. 1 Xicaochang, Haidian District, Beijing.
Legal Representative: Chen Chongyu, Chairman of the Board.
Agent ad litem: Zhang Chenyang, Attorney at Beijing Gaotong Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Zhang Xiaozhe, Attorney at Beijing Gaotong Law Firm.

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): China Huarong Asset Management Corporation. Domicile: No. 10 Baiyun Road, Xicheng District, Beijing.
Legal Representative: Yang Kaisheng, President of the Corporation.
Agent ad litem: Li Dan, Employee of the Corporation.
Agent ad litem: Yang Huaijun, Employee of the Corporation.

The appellant Beijing Xin'ao'te Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xin'ao'te Group), in dispute with the appellant China Huarong Asset Management Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Huarong Company) over an equity transfer contract, appealed to this Court against the Civil Judgment (2003) Gao Min Chu Zi No. 1 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court. This Court accepted the case on August 14, 2003, and formed a collegial panel composed of Presiding Judge Xu Ruibai and Acting Judges Wang Xiansen and Yang Yongmei to conduct the trial. The court clerk Kong Ling kept the record. The trial of this case is now concluded.

The following facts were found by the court of first instance:

On June 28, 2002, Huarong Company, a third party Bit Technology Holding Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Bit Technology), and Xin'ao'te Group signed an equity transfer agreement concerning Beijing Bei Guang Electronic Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Bei Guang Group). The main contents of the agreement were as follows: Bit Technology and Xin'ao'te Group jointly formed a purchasing group to acquire the 55.081% equity in Bei Guang Group held by Huarong Company, with the final price of the equity transfer not less than RMB 300 million. The payment for the equity transfer was to be made in installments. Within three days after the signing of the agreement, Bit Technology and Xin'ao'te Group were to pay RMB 100 million into an account designated by Huarong Company, and the remaining amount was to be paid within three months after the signing of the agreement or within seven days after the appraisal report was filed with the competent state authority. After Bit Technology and Xin'ao'te Group paid RMB 100 million in accordance with the agreement, Huarong Company was to assist in handling the procedures for the transfer of the equity. The transferees fully understood the risk that other shareholders might not cooperate in handling the change of registration for the equity with the industry and commerce authorities, and undertook not to raise any objections to the transferor in this regard, and such circumstances were not to affect the transferees' payment of the equity transfer price, and the equity transfer price already received by the transferor was not to be returned. In addition, the agreement also stipulated matters such as equity pledge, liability for breach, and applicable law. On the same day (June 28, 2002), upon the proposal of Huarong Company, the first temporary shareholders' meeting of Bei Guang Group for the year 2002 was convened to make a resolution on the matters related to Huarong Company's transfer of all its equity in Bei Guang Group to the purchasing group composed of Bit Technology and Xin'ao'te Group in a single transaction. Another shareholder of Bei Guang Group, Beijing Electronic Holding Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Electronic Company), did not sign and seal to approve the relevant resolution. On September 27, 2002, Huarong Company, a third party Xinjiang International Trust and Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xinjiang International Trust), Xin'ao'te Group, and Bit Technology; and Huarong Company, Xin'ao'te Group, and Bit Technology entered into two separate Agreements on Issues Related to Equity Transfer (I) and (II) respectively. The facts confirmed by these two agreements were mainly that Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology had delivered a total of RMB 100 million in equity transfer payments to Huarong Company on July 22, August 6, and August 30 of the same year. Xinjiang International Trust agreed to provide financing support to Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology in the form of a trust, and was to remit a total of RMB 200 million into the designated account before 12:00 noon on September 28 of the same year. The agreements also stipulated that because another shareholder of Bei Guang Group had initiated arbitration proceedings on the ground that Huarong Company had violated its preemptive right, Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology agreed to make a commitment to continue performing the equity transfer agreement of June 28 of the same year. Specifically, if Huarong Company lost in the arbitration case, resulting in the inability to transfer the equity or continue performing the equity transfer agreement, Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology would not hold Huarong Company liable for any interest, financing costs, expected profits, compensation, or other related responsibilities that might or should arise from signing the above agreements with respect to the RMB 200 million in funds. Additionally, the agreements stipulated other obligations that Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology were to perform under the above conditions. On December 10 of the same year, Xinjiang International Trust, Xin'ao'te Group, and Bit Technology jointly sent a letter to Huarong Company, requesting that Huarong Company, before the relevant deadline, complete all procedures for withdrawing an amount equivalent to RMB 200 million from the joint account of the funds and pay RMB 5 million to Xinjiang International Trust out of the RMB 100 million paid by Xin'ao'te Group to Huarong Company. Huarong Company acted in accordance with this letter. Subsequently, the Beijing office of Huarong Company sent a letter to Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology requesting the refund of the remaining amount of RMB 95.5 million (including an advance payment of RMB 500,000 for the equity transfer project), and, along with notarial staff from the Second Notary Public Office of Beijing, delivered a notice of refund, but received no response. Xin'ao'te Group denied receiving any of the above refund notices. On April 16, 2003, Huarong Company returned the equity transfer payment of RMB 95.5 million paid by Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology to Xin'ao'te Group's account.

Bit Technology issued a Power of Attorney to Xin'ao'te Group, stating that Bit Technology fully authorized Xin'ao'te Group to hold the 0.5% equity in Bei Guang Group that Bit Technology had lawfully acquired, to exercise all shareholders' rights corresponding to such equity, and to perform the corresponding obligations.

On September 23, 2002, Electronic Company, as the applicant, filed an application with the Beijing Arbitration Commission against Huarong Company as the respondent, seeking a ruling that Electronic Company, as a shareholder of Bei Guang Group, was entitled to a preemptive right. On December 9 of the same year, the Beijing Arbitration Commission rendered a final award, the main content of which was: "By December 31, 2002, Electronic Company has the right to exercise its preemptive right to purchase the 55% equity in Bei Guang Group that Huarong Company intends to transfer, under the same conditions. The total transfer price of RMB 300 million shall be paid in a lump sum to Huarong Company by December 31, 2002." Pursuant to this award, on December 20 of the same year, Electronic Company and Huarong Company entered into an agreement; on December 23 of the same year, Electronic Company made the payment to Huarong Company.

Because the equity transfer agreement between Huarong Company and Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology could not be further performed, Xin'ao'te Group filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance on December 19 of the same year, requesting that the court order Huarong Company to continue performing the equity transfer agreement; to compensate for losses of RMB 19,816,077 incurred due to the breach of the equity transfer agreement; and to bear the litigation costs and attorneys' fees.

The court of first instance held that the equity transfer agreement concerning Bei Guang Group signed by Huarong Company, Bit Technology, and Xin'ao'te Group on June 28, 2002, reflected the true intentions of all parties, and the signatories should have performed it in accordance with the agreement. However, since the Beijing Arbitration Commission had rendered a binding award prior to this case, ruling that another shareholder of Bei Guang Group, Electronic Company, was entitled to a preemptive right to purchase the equity Huarong Company intended to transfer under the same conditions, and because Electronic Company and Huarong Company had entered into an agreement and made payment within the time specified in the arbitration award, the purpose of the equity transfer agreement between Huarong Company, Bit Technology, and Xin'ao'te Group could no longer be achieved, and the basic conditions for performing the contract no longer existed. Therefore, the contract should be terminated. Accordingly, Xin'ao'te Group's claim for continued performance of the equity transfer agreement was not supported. Huarong Company, knowing that Electronic Company had explicitly expressed its disagreement with the transfer of the equity, had not clearly waived its purchase right, and had not signed or sealed the relevant shareholders' resolution to approve the equity transfer, was aware of the possibility that the equity transfer agreement might be incapable of performance. Nevertheless, it still entered into the equity transfer agreement and multiple ancillary agreements with Xin'ao'te Group and, after Electronic Company applied for arbitration, still accepted RMB 200 million in equity transfer payments. Huarong Company bore primary responsibility for the dispute and should bear the corresponding consequences. Xin'ao'te Group, in the course of contracting with Huarong Company, was aware of the uncertain status of the equity to be purchased and the associated risks, and should also bear corresponding responsibility for some of the losses arising from the inability to perform the equity transfer agreement. Xin'ao'te Group's claims for compensation for the profits it might have obtained had the equity transfer agreement been normally performed and for the relevant expenses of the acquisition project team were not supported. The losses incurred by Xin'ao'te Group from the payments made to facilitate the performance of the agreement and to achieve the contract's purpose should be compensated by Huarong Company. Given that the parties had no specific agreement on this matter and could not reach a consensus, based on the circumstances of the parties' performance of the contract, the reasonable losses that had already occurred, and the parties' respective responsibilities in this case, it was appropriate to determine that Huarong Company should compensate Xin'ao'te Group for losses in the amount of RMB 3 million. In accordance with Article 91 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of first instance ruled as follows: 1. The equity transfer agreement and related agreements concerning Beijing Bei Guang Electronic Group Co., Ltd., signed by Huarong Company, Bit Technology, and Xin'ao'te Group, were terminated. 2. Huarong Company was to compensate Xin'ao'te Group for losses of RMB 3 million (to be paid within ten days from the effective date of the judgment; if overdue, overdue fines were to be paid in accordance with the relevant provisions of the People's Bank of China). Court acceptance fee of RMB 1,510,010 and preservation fee of RMB 1,501,020 for the first instance were all borne by Huarong Company.

Huarong Company, dissatisfied with the above civil judgment of the court of first instance, appealed to this Court, arguing: The court of first instance erred in ordering Huarong Company to bear compensation liability without legal basis. Huarong Company had no fault whatsoever regarding the inability to perform the equity transfer agreement. Huarong Company had taken a series of measures to protect Electronic Company's preemptive right. Before the arbitration award, Huarong Company believed that the equity transfer and the change of registration fully complied with the relevant legal provisions. Xin'ao'te Group was aware of and acknowledged the measures taken by Huarong Company, and it too believed that Electronic Company had waived its preemptive right. Because the Beijing Arbitration Commission ruled that Electronic Company was entitled to a preemptive right to purchase the equity Huarong Company intended to transfer under the same conditions, Huarong Company's inability to continue performing the equity transfer agreement with Xin'ao'te Group due to compliance with the binding arbitration award was not its fault, and it should not bear Xin'ao'te Group's losses. Huarong Company had truthfully informed Xin'ao'te Group of the status of the equity assets and the risks associated with the equity transfer. Xin'ao'te Group fully understood, was aware of, and accepted the risks of the equity transfer. The parties agreed that the risk of failure to transfer the equity was to be borne by Xin'ao'te Group, and Huarong Company should not be held liable for damages for the termination of the equity transfer agreement. The court of first instance, while dismissing Xin'ao'te Group's main claims, ordered Huarong Company to bear all litigation costs, which was unfair. Therefore, Huarong Company requested the reversal of Item 2 of the principal text of the original judgment, the dismissal of Huarong Company's liability, and that Xin'ao'te Group bear the acceptance fees and preservation fees for both the first and second instances.

Xin'ao'te Group, also dissatisfied with the above civil judgment of the court of first instance, appealed to this Court, arguing: 1. The responsibility for the inability to perform the equity transfer agreement lay with Huarong Company, and Huarong Company should bear liability for damages. According to the equity transfer agreement, Huarong Company warranted that it held complete and exclusive rights to the equity in Bei Guang Group, and that no pledges or other third-party encumbrances were attached to such equity. However, Electronic Company's exercise of its preemptive right indicated that the equity had not excluded the preemptive right and was not complete and exclusive. 2. Huarong Company's claim for exemption from liability on the ground that Electronic Company had a preemptive right was legally unfounded. Huarong Company could not rely on the first clause of the Agreement on Issues Related to Equity Transfer (II) to exempt itself from liability for damages. That clause provided that if Huarong Company lost in the arbitration case, resulting in the inability to transfer the equity or continue performing the equity transfer agreement, Xin'ao'te Group would not hold Huarong Company liable for any interest, financing costs, expected profits, compensation, or other related responsibilities that might or should arise from signing the equity transfer agreement and the Agreement on Issues Related to Equity Transfer (I) with respect to the RMB 200 million in funds. The arbitration did not rule that Huarong Company must transfer the equity to Electronic Company, nor did it necessarily cause the equity to be unable to be transferred to Xin'ao'te Group's name. Moreover, the arbitration award required Electronic Company to exercise its preemptive right at a price of RMB 300 million, while the equity transfer agreement between Xin'ao'te Group and Huarong Company specified RMB 300 million as the minimum purchase price, with no maximum cap. Huarong Company should have continued to perform its equity transfer agreement with Xin'ao'te Group by providing Xin'ao'te Group and Electronic Company with a fair, open, and just opportunity to compete. Only if Xin'ao'te Group abandoned the competition with Electronic Company would Huarong Company be entitled to stop performing the equity transfer agreement. Otherwise, Huarong Company constituted a breach of contract and should bear the resulting liability. Huarong Company now deliberately refuses to perform the equity transfer agreement, causing significant losses to Xin'ao'te Group, and Huarong Company is not entitled to rely on the agreement to exempt itself from liability for the losses arising from its acceptance of RMB 200 million from Xin'ao'te Group. 3. The amount of compensation determined by the court of first instance lacked a basis. The parties did not exempt the losses arising from the RMB 100 million in funds. Huarong Company should compensate Xin'ao'te Group for total losses of RMB 19,816,077, including: fees paid to Xinjiang International Trust of RMB 6,435,750; loan interest payable to a third party, Jinxin Trust and Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jinxin Trust) of RMB 3,044,884.93; financial advisory fees of RMB 2,248,265.75; consulting fees paid to Wanshan Management Co., Ltd. of RMB 2 million; audit fees paid to Mingze Accounting Firm of RMB 55,000; equity returns that could have been obtained from August to December 2002 of RMB 4.59 million; salaries for personnel engaged in the equity acquisition of RMB 502,590; and other losses of RMB 939,586.32. Therefore, Xin'ao'te Group requested the reversal of Item 2 of the principal text of the original judgment, ordering Huarong Company to compensate Xin'ao'te Group for losses of RMB 19,816,077, and that Huarong Company bear the litigation costs and preservation fees for both the first and second instances.

In addition to the facts found by the court of first instance, this Court also found the following:

On June 12, 2002, Xin'ao'te Group's attorney sent a lawyer's letter to Huarong Company, stating that Xin'ao'te Group had signed an Equity Transfer Framework Agreement with Huarong Company in December 2001 regarding the equity transfer, and that on April 15, 2002, Huarong Company had formally notified Electronic Company by a "Notice Letter" of the relevant circumstances of the equity transfer, the proposed percentage of equity to be transferred, the transfer price, the payment term, etc., and had requested Electronic Company to respond definitively on whether it would exercise its preemptive right under the above conditions by April 24 of the same year, with the consequence that if Electronic Company failed to clearly indicate its intention to acquire by that date, it would lose its preemptive right. Electronic Company replied that it did not waive its preemptive right. The lawyer's letter argued that Electronic Company's statement that it did not waive its preemptive right did not meet Huarong Company's requirement for a "clear indication of whether to acquire or not," and that its counter-request regarding the transfer conditions amounted to a rejection of the same conditions, thus Electronic Company had lost its preemptive right, and Huarong Company had no need, nor should it, further discuss the preemptive right with Electronic Company. The lawyer's letter concluded that the substantive conditions for Huarong Company to enter into the equity transfer contract with the transferees Bit Technology and Xin'ao'te Group had been determined, and the procedural requirements had been satisfied. On June 13 of the same year, Huarong Company sent a "Notice Letter" to Electronic Company through notarization, again notifying it of the conditions for the equity transfer reached with Xin'ao'te Group and others, and requested Electronic Company to provide a written undertaking before 9:00 a.m. on June 28 of the same year on whether it would exercise its preemptive right under the same conditions; if it undertook to exercise the right, it should sign an equity transfer agreement on the same day; otherwise, it would be deemed to have waived the preemptive right. Electronic Company did not respond to this notice. Huarong Company signed the equity transfer agreement with Xin'ao'te Group and Bit Technology at 11:30 a.m. on June 28 of the same year. Clause 6.1 of that agreement provided: If Bei Guang Group and other shareholders of Bei Guang Group do not cooperate with the transferee in handling the change of registration for the equity with the industry and commerce authorities, this may result in a delay in the change of registration and the inability to promptly transfer the transferor's equity to the transferee's name. The transferee is fully aware of the aforementioned risk, and the transferor assumes no responsibility for the risks that may arise from this. Clause 7.1 provided: Huarong Company warrants that it has complete and exclusive rights to the equity in Bei Guang Group; as of the effective date of this agreement, no pledges or other third-party encumbrances are attached to such equity. Thereafter, Huarong Company and Xin'ao'te Group began to perform their respective obligations under the transfer agreement. Xin'ao'te Group paid transfer payments of RMB 20 million, RMB 10 million, and RMB 70 million to Huarong Company on July 22, August 6, and August 30 of the same year, respectively. On September 2 of the same year, Huarong Company sent a letter to Bei Guang Group, requesting that Bei Guang Group assist in handling the procedures for the equity transfer registration. On December 18 of the same year, Huarong Company, at Xin'ao'te Group's request, paid RMB 5 million to Xinjiang International Trust out of the RMB 100 million that Xin'ao'te Group had paid to Huarong Company.

On April 15, 2002, Xin'ao'te Group entered into an agreement with a third party, Wanshan Management Co., Ltd., stipulating that Xin'ao'te Group retained Wanshan Management as a consulting advisor for the acquisition of the target assets. Xin'ao'te Group was to pay an initial consulting fee of RMB 2 million to Wanshan Management; if the acquisition was unsuccessful for reasons not attributable to Xin'ao'te Group, Wanshan Management would refund RMB 1 million to Xin'ao'te Group. On the same day, Wanshan Management issued a receipt acknowledging receipt of RMB 2 million from Xin'ao'te Group. On August 29 of the same year, Xin'ao'te Group and Jinxin Trust entered into a working capital loan agreement, stipulating a loan amount of RMB 70 million, an interest rate of 5.2525 per mille per month, and a loan term from August 29 of the same year to September 29 of the same year. On the same day, Xin'ao'te Group and Jinxin Trust entered into a Project Financing Financial Advisory Agreement, stipulating that Jinxin Trust would provide financing consultation for Xin'ao'te Group's project to acquire 55% of Bei Guang Group's equity, formulate specific financing plans, etc. The financial advisory service period was from August 29 of the same year to June 29, 2003, and Xin'ao'te Group was to pay corresponding financial advisory fees of RMB 2.98 million. On September 5, 2003, Jinxin Trust demanded payment of loan interest of RMB 3,044,884.93 and financial advisory fees of RMB 2,248,265.75 from Xin'ao'te Group. On September 25, 2002, Beijing Mingze Accounting Firm, upon the entrustment of Xin'ao'te Group, issued an audit report on Bei Guang Group, which stated that Bei Guang Group's net profit from January to August 2002 was RMB 4,024,318.56. Xin'ao'te Group held two invoices issued by Beijing Mingze Accounting Firm on October 22, 2002, in the amount of RMB 55,000. Xin'ao'te Group paid a total of RMB 386,490 in wages for the acquisition team personnel from April to December 2002.

During the trial of this case, Xin'ao'te Group adduced evidence to explain that its name had been changed from "Beijing Xin'ao'te Group" to "Beijing Xin'ao'te Group Co., Ltd."

Opinion of the Court: The equity transfer agreement entered into by Huarong Company, New Auto Group, and Bit Technology represents the true expression of the parties' intent, does not violate the prohibitive provisions of relevant laws and administrative regulations, and is thus a valid contract. The reason for the failure to continue performance of the equity transfer agreement was that the effective arbitral award of the Beijing Arbitration Commission ruled that a third party, Electronics Company, had a preemptive right to purchase the equity to be transferred by Huarong Company on the same terms, and that Electronics Company and Huarong Company, within the time specified in the arbitral award, entered into an agreement and paid RMB 300 million to Huarong Company as payment for the equity transfer. The actual exercise of the preemptive right by Electronics Company rendered the subject matter of the equity transfer agreement between Huarong Company and New Auto Group non-existent, making further performance impossible. The original trial judgment ordering the termination of the equity transfer agreement was not improper, and neither party appealed this issue; therefore, this Court affirms that part of the judgment.

One of the focal points of the dispute in this case is how the losses caused to New Auto Group by the termination of the equity transfer agreement should be allocated. When Huarong Company and New Auto Group entered into the equity transfer agreement, both were aware that other shareholders under the Company Law have a preemptive right to purchase on the same terms, and were also aware of Electronics Company's position of not waiving its preemptive right. Since the law does not provide clear provisions on the manner and time limit for shareholders to exercise the preemptive right, Huarong Company used a notice to set a deadline for Electronics Company to exercise its preemptive right, with the consequence that failure to do so within the deadline would be deemed a waiver. New Auto Group fully agreed that Huarong Company had, by this method, eliminated Electronics Company's right to exercise its preemptive right. Both parties entered into the equity transfer agreement under the belief that Electronics Company had lost its preemptive right. The subsequent arbitral award did not support the judgment of Huarong Company and New Auto Group on the preemptive right issue, but ruled that Electronics Company was entitled to exercise its preemptive right. The actual exercise of the preemptive right by Electronics Company ultimately led to the termination of the equity transfer agreement in this case. Since Huarong Company and New Auto Group, at the time of contracting, should have foreseen that the contract might be terminated due to Electronics Company's exercise of its preemptive right, but did not, causing the termination of the contract, both parties are at fault. The losses incurred by New Auto Group in preparing for and actually performing the contract shall be borne 50% each by Huarong Company and New Auto Group. The original trial judgment found that Huarong Company's responsibility was greater than that of New Auto Group, which does not align with the facts; this Court hereby corrects that. Huarong Company's argument that its compliance with the effective arbitral award made it unable to continue performing the equity transfer agreement with New Auto Group, that it had no fault, and that it should not bear the losses of New Auto Group, is inconsistent with the facts; this Court does not support it. Huarong Company's claim that, based on the agreement's provision that the risk of failure to transfer the equity is borne by New Auto Group, it should not be liable for the losses caused by termination, cannot be sustained because the agreement between Huarong Company and New Auto Group only stipulated the risk of delayed transfer, not the risk of failure to transfer. Therefore, this ground of appeal by Huarong Company also fails, and this Court does not support it. The preemptive right is a right granted by law to shareholders to purchase, on the same terms, shares that other shareholders intend to transfer to outsiders; it is a right designed to ensure the personal nature of a limited liability company. The provision on the preemptive right is not a restriction on the equity rights of the shareholder intending to transfer shares or a limitation on their freedom to transfer shares. Electronics Company's lawful exercise of its preemptive right does not prove that Huarong Company does not have a complete and exclusive right over the equity it holds. New Auto Group's appeal request for Huarong Company to bear full compensation liability on the ground that Huarong Company breached the agreement lacks factual and legal basis; this Court does not support it.

Another focal point of the dispute in this case is the calculation of losses caused by the termination of the equity transfer agreement. First, regarding the issue of New Auto Group's loss from the payment of RMB 200 million as equity transfer price. The "Agreement Related to the Equity Transfer Issues (II)" clearly stipulates that if Huarong Company loses the arbitration case, resulting in the failure to transfer the equity and the inability to continue the equity transfer agreement, New Auto Group shall not hold Huarong Company liable for any responsibility that may or might arise concerning interest, financing costs, expected profits, compensation, etc., related to the RMB 200 million fund. This agreement represents the true expression of the parties' intent, does not violate relevant laws and administrative regulations, and should be valid. The premise of this exemption is Huarong Company's loss in the arbitration, not, as argued by New Auto Group, that even in the event of Huarong Company's loss, New Auto Group and Electronics Company should engage in a further bidding process. New Auto Group's act of recovering the RMB 200 million fund immediately after Huarong Company lost the arbitration also indicates that it had no intention to engage in further bidding. New Auto Group's voluntary waiver of compensation related to the RMB 200 million is an act of disposing of its own rights. Therefore, this Court does not support New Auto Group's appeal request that Huarong Company should compensate it for the loss of RMB 6,435,750 caused by the payment of RMB 200 million as equity transfer price. Second, regarding the loss incurred by New Auto Group due to the payment of RMB 100 million as equity transfer price. How to raise the equity transfer price is New Auto Group's own conduct; the sources of funds may be various. The reasonable loss that Huarong Company could have foreseen is only the interest loss during the period it actually possessed the funds, not the actual costs incurred by New Auto Group for external financing. Therefore, this part of the loss should be calculated based on the time and amount of funds actually in Huarong Company's possession, at the six-month fixed deposit rate of the People's Bank of China. Third, the consulting fees, audit fees, financial advisory fees, personnel wages, etc., paid by New Auto Group to perform the contract are payments actually made or necessarily to be made by it in good faith to achieve the contract's purpose; these should be recognized as losses arising from the failure to perform the contract. Among these, RMB 2 million in consulting fees has been paid, but under New Auto Group's contract with Wanmei Management Co., Ltd., New Auto Group is entitled to demand a refund of RMB 1 million from Wanmei Management. Therefore, the actual loss for consulting fees should be recognized as RMB 1 million. The loss for personnel wages should be calculated based on the personnel actually engaged in the equity acquisition and the time involved, totaling RMB 386,490. The audit fees are calculated at the actually paid amount of RMB 55,000. The financial advisory fees are calculated at the amount of RMB 2,248,265.75 that was claimed from New Auto Group. The total loss from the aforementioned consulting fees, audit fees, financial advisory fees, and personnel wages amounts to RMB 3,689,755.75, of which Huarong Company bears 50%, i.e., RMB 1,844,877.88. New Auto Group's claim for equity income of RMB 4.59 million is not supported due to insufficient evidence; this Court does not uphold it.

In summary, the original trial judgment did not specifically determine the amount of New Auto Group's losses and improperly determined the proportion of responsibility that Huarong Company should bear; this Court hereby corrects that. New Auto Group's appeal ground that it should receive loss compensation of RMB 19,816,077 cannot be sustained; this Court does not support it. Huarong Company's appeal ground that it should not bear compensation liability also cannot be sustained; this Court does not support it. Pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Items (1) and (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court renders the following judgment:

1. Affirm Item 1 of the main text of the civil judgment (2003) Gao Min Chu Zi No. 1 of the Beijing High People's Court.

2. Amend Item 2 of the main text of the civil judgment (2003) Gao Min Chu Zi No. 1 of the Beijing High People's Court to: China Huarong Asset Management Company shall compensate Beijing New Auto Group Co., Ltd. for losses of RMB 1,844,877.88 and 50% of the interest loss on the RMB 100 million fund (the interest shall be calculated based on the People's Bank of China's six-month fixed deposit rate for the same period, segmented by the time and amount of actual possession of the funds: RMB 20 million from July 22, 2002 to December 18, 2002; RMB 15 million from December 19, 2002 to April 16, 2003; RMB 10 million from August 6, 2002 to April 16, 2003; RMB 70 million from August 30, 2002 to April 16, 2003).

The above payment shall be made within 10 days from the day following the service of this judgment. If payment is overdue, it shall be handled in accordance with Article 232 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

The first instance case acceptance fee of RMB 1,510,010 shall be borne 50% each by China Huarong Asset Management Company and Beijing New Auto Group Co., Ltd., i.e., RMB 755,005 each; the property preservation fee of RMB 1,501,020 shall be borne 50% each by China Huarong Asset Management Company and Beijing New Auto Group Co., Ltd., i.e., RMB 750,510 each; the second instance case acceptance fee of RMB 109,090 shall be borne 50% each by China Huarong Asset Management Company and Beijing New Auto Group Co., Ltd., i.e., RMB 54,545 each.

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Xu Ruibai

Acting Judge: Wang Xiansen

Acting Judge: Yang Yongmei

November 7, 2003

Clerk: Kong Ling

[Profile of the Presiding Judge]

Xu Ruibai, Senior Judge: Born in 1963, Bachelor of Laws, served as a judge of the Supreme People's Court since 1994.
